chunk-001:c001.proposition: The mythicist thesis allows Jesus a mortal Jewish body while locating his death and resurrection in a heavenly mythic realm comparable to celestial salvific events in ancient cults.

orphanFallback.rationale: Carrier presents this as a standalone definition of his thesis and grounds its heavenly setting through comparison with ancient savior-cult narratives.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Paul's authentic letters never unambiguously state where Jesus was born, lived, died, buried, or resurrected, leaving their cosmic account compatible with a heavenly setting.

orphanFallback.rationale: The passage independently advances the textual premise that Paul's letters omit an explicit earthly location for the events and consistently give them cosmic significance.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: The rulers who crucified Jesus are more plausibly demonic powers because their concealed cosmic knowledge and effort to thwart God's plan fit celestial agents better than Paul's God-appointed human rulers.

orphanFallback.rationale: Even without a retained opposing move, Carrier's comparison of First Corinthians with Romans supplies an affirmative textual case for identifying the rulers as demonic powers.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: A celestial crucifixion was intelligible in ancient Jewish cosmology because heavenly realms could contain copies of earthly things and demonic agents could enact the corresponding execution there.

orphanFallback.rationale: Carrier's appeal to heavenly counterparts of earthly objects and practices supplies a self-contained cosmological mechanism for crucifixion in the proposed mythic realm.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Paul's expression brother of the Lord can denote an ordinary baptized Christian, and the wording in Galatians does not clearly identify James as Jesus's biological sibling.

orphanFallback.rationale: Carrier independently grounds the non-biological reading in the status of baptized Christians as the Lord's brethren and in Paul's apostolic-status discussion.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-04.proposition: First Corinthians 9 remains ambiguous between baptized and biological brothers, while later Gospel family traditions cannot establish which meaning Paul intended.

orphanFallback.rationale: The move stands constructively as a source-order argument: Paul's own vague wording must be interpreted independently of later family narratives that he does not mention.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-05.proposition: Acts is agenda-driven fictionalized history, and any skeleton of sourced information cannot be cleanly separated from the author's embellishments and alterations.

orphanFallback.rationale: Carrier offers this as his affirmative account of Acts, identifying its apologetic agendas while allowing uncertain source material beneath the crafted narrative.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: Accurate incidental details do not validate Acts because its chronology, account of Paul's mission, and portrayal of the Torah-free gospel conflict with Paul's own letters.

orphanFallback.rationale: The cited contrasts concerning Arabia, Judea, the Gentile mission, Peter, and chronology form an independent affirmative case against treating Acts as reliable Pauline testimony.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-05.proposition: John's use and rewriting of earlier Gospels explains apparent interlocking details as designed literary correspondences rather than independent historical corroboration.

orphanFallback.rationale: Carrier supplies literary dependence as a positive explanatory model in which John deliberately reworks prior Gospel material to shape and clarify his own narrative.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-07.proposition: An author adapting source material can select characters appropriate to its setting without restating every background detail, so omission of the location does not establish independence.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source-use mechanism is independently substantive: an adapting author may inherit contextual associations when choosing characters without explicitly reproducing the source's geography.
